newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Strong Australia jobs rise seen, but market weak.
newsitem.headline: Strong Australia jobs rise seen, but market weak.

text.p: Australia's June labour force data should produce a strong set of headlines, but economists said that if the rise came in as forecast it would do little to change the underlying picture of a still subdued jobs market.
As a result, Thursday's expected 40,000-plus rise would not do any serious damage to the case for an interest rate cut, as it would still leave the unemployment rate stubbornly above 8.5 percent.

"Even with a sharp rise in employment in June, the underlying tone of the labour market is undeniably soft, and the leading indicators point to only modest improvement in the coming months," Hambros fixed income economist Su-Lin Ong said.
The median forecast of economists surveyed by Reuters was for employment to rise by 42,500. Forecasts ranged from a rise of 25,000 to a rise of 60,000.
For unemployment a slight improvement to 8.7 percent was forecast for June, down from 8.8 percent in May.

Jobs have become both a political and financial markets focus over the last year, with Prime Minister John Howard announcing on Tuesday that had a called a special cabinet meeting in August to focus on the unemployment rate.
"I think it is very important that we dedicate an entire cabinet day to discussing that issue, it is an enormously important issue," Howard said in a radio interview.

For markets, the stalled labour market is seen as a sign that there could be another rate cut on the way. A rise in line with forecasts is seen as neutral for the markets, and would still leave the market still looking for a cut.
A jobs rise below expectations, or a fall, would be very bullish for those looking for an rate cut in July or August.
"If employment falls again we would take the probability of a rate cut later this month from 40 percent to 90 percent," HSBC Markets chief economist John Edwards said.
However, the risk to forecasts after the recent run of soft jobs data is seen to the topside, although it would take a large rise to alter perceptions of a still weak labour market.

"An employment rise in the order of 70,000 or more, mostly in full-time employment, would need to occur to materially alter the picture of labour market weakness," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.

With employment growth stalled -- a rise of 42,500 would mean that employment had risen by under 4,500 jobs per month iver the first half of 1997 -- the unemployment rate has similarly remained stalled above 8.5 percent.
When the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) cut rates on July 31 last year, it cited the high unemployment rate as a supporting factor.
"The earlier downtrend in unemployment has largely stalled over the past year, at around 8.5 percent," the RBA said last July.
Since then, the stalled labour market has been a factor behind the three further rate cuts the RBA had delivered, but as yet they have not had much of a labour market impact.
If unemployment comes in as forcast at 8.7 percent, it will mean that for 11 of the 12 months of the 1996/97 (July/June) fiscal year, unemployment has been at 8.6 percent or higher.

While employment was expected to bounce back in June and forward indicators were suggesting some improvement in the pace of employment growth, it was still not fast enough to make sizeable inroads into the unemployment rate in coming months.

"This month is likely to rebound from last month, which is likely to see a modest upwards trend in emloyment, not enough to see enough to see unemployment trend down," Rothschild Australia chief economist Ric Simes said.
"Rather it looks like staying at around 8.75 percent for the next few months." -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
